content: In scientific contexts, the term transdisciplinarity is employed in various ways. In German-speaking countries, it is predominantly used to describe integrative forms of research, as noted by Mittelstrass in 2003. This interpretation contrasts with the understanding of transdisciplinarity as a principle aimed at achieving a unity of knowledge that transcends disciplinary boundaries, as described by Nicolescu in 2002. Transdisciplinarity, when viewed as an integrative research principle, encompasses a range of methodologies designed to connect scientific knowledge with non-scientific experiences and practices in the context of problem-solving. This approach focuses on addressing real-world issues rather than merely engaging in debates about the origins and relevance of problems within scientific discourse. A critical aspect of transdisciplinary research is the extent to which it integrates diverse scientific perspectives. This feature is often used to differentiate transdisciplinarity from interdisciplinarity and multidisciplinarity. However, due to the varying and sometimes inconsistent concepts and terminologies associated with transdisciplinary research, structuring this field can be challenging. For instance, a 2003 conference in Göttingen attempted to illustrate the broad spectrum of understandings of multi-, inter-, and transdisciplinarity, proposing ways to converge these concepts without discarding existing usages. Pohl and Hirsch Hadorn (2007) also provided an overview of terminology and suggested a more systematic application of key terms. In the context of integrative research, transdisciplinarity is particularly relevant in situations where knowledge about societal issues is uncertain, the nature of the problems is contested, and the stakes for involved actors are high, as described by Funtowicz and Ravetz in 1993. In such scenarios, transdisciplinary research becomes essential because it is not immediately clear what the most pertinent problems are or how they can be structured and transformed into productive research questions. Three primary types of research questions arise in transdisciplinary contexts. The first type pertains to empirical processes that have led to the current problems and may influence their future development, referred to as system knowledge. The second type involves questions about values and norms that are acceptable as a foundation for determining the appropriate goals of the problem-solving process, known as target knowledge. The third type addresses whether and how a given problem situation can be transformed and improved, termed transformation knowledge. To address these research questions effectively in a transdisciplinary manner, several requirements must be met. These include adequately addressing the complexity of problems, considering the diversity of life-world and scientific perceptions of problems, linking abstract and case-specific knowledge, and developing knowledge and practices that promote what is perceived as the common good. These principles are highlighted by Hirsch Hadorn et al. (2008) and Jaeger & Scheringer (1998). A transdisciplinary research approach can only emerge if participating experts engage in open discussion and dialogue, respecting each perspective as equally important and relating the different perspectives to one another. However, working in a transdisciplinary manner is challenging because scientists often feel overwhelmed by the volume of information in everyday practice and the incommensurability of specialized languages across fields of expertise. Therefore, individuals with skills in moderation, mediation, association, and knowledge transfer are essential to initiate and sustain a critical yet constructive dialogue. These individuals must also possess in-depth knowledge and expertise in the disciplines involved. A different perspective on transdisciplinarity was developed in 1987 by 163 researchers from the International Center for Transdisciplinary Research (CIRET). A Charter of Transdisciplinarity was adopted at the 1st World Congress of Transdisciplinarity in Portugal in 1994. In the CIRET approach, transdisciplinarity is fundamentally distinct from interdisciplinarity. Interdisciplinarity involves the transfer of methods from one discipline to another. While interdisciplinarity and multidisciplinarity extend beyond disciplinary boundaries, their goals remain within the framework of disciplinary research. In contrast, as the prefix trans suggests, transdisciplinarity concerns what lies between, across, and beyond individual disciplines. Its goal is to understand the present world, with one of its imperatives being the overarching unity of knowledge. Basarab Nicolescu defines transdisciplinarity through three methodological postulates: the existence of levels of Reality, the logic of the included middle, and complexity. In the presence of multiple levels of Reality, the space between and beyond disciplines is rich with information. Disciplinary research typically focuses on a single level of Reality or fragments of one level. Conversely, transdisciplinarity addresses the dynamics generated by the interaction of multiple levels of Reality simultaneously. Discovering these dynamics necessarily involves disciplinary knowledge. While transdisciplinarity is not a new discipline or super-discipline, it is nourished by disciplinary research, which, in turn, is enriched by transdisciplinary knowledge in a fertile and innovative manner. Thus, disciplinary and transdisciplinary research are not antagonistic but complementary. Similarly, transdisciplinary research complements, rather than opposes, multidisciplinarity and interdisciplinarity. However, transdisciplinarity is fundamentally distinct from the latter two due to its goal of understanding the present world, which cannot be achieved within the framework of disciplinary research. The objectives of multidisciplinarity and interdisciplinarity always remain within the boundaries of disciplinary research. The frequent confusion between transdisciplinarity, interdisciplinarity, and multidisciplinarity—partly because all three transcend disciplinary boundaries—obscures the significant potential of transdisciplinarity. Transdisciplinarity is also evident in the arts and humanities. For example, in art and design, the research approach of the Planetary Collegium seeks to develop transdisciplinary discourse at the convergence of art, science, technology, and consciousness research. In this framework, all anthropological disciplines, their questions, and results can be interconnected and allocated to one another. This chart includes all realms of anthropological research, serving as a starting point for systematically organizing all human sciences and providing a foundation for consistent networking and structuring of their results. This bio-psycho-social orientation framework underpins the development of the Fundamental Theory of Human Sciences and fosters a transdisciplinary consensus. In this tabulated orientation matrix, the questions and reference levels in italics also pertain to the humanities.
